content.stem: X-rays and gamma rays are both:
options: Electromagnetic radiation (photons)
Fast-moving charged particles here
Plain audible sound waves only here
Free neutron particles only here, oddly
content.explanation: X-rays and gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation (photons) with no mass and no charge; they differ in origin, not in fundamental nature.
distractors: Photons carry no electric charge, unlike alpha or beta particles.
Radiation used in RT is electromagnetic, not acoustic like ultrasound.
Neutrons are particles used in neutron radiography, a separate method.

content.stem: The fundamental difference between X-rays and gamma rays is that:
options: X-rays originate outside the nucleus; gamma rays originate within the nucleus
X-rays are particles while gamma rays are simple waves here, somehow quite oddly
Gamma rays have no energy at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough now
X-rays simply cannot expose any film here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: X-rays are produced when fast electrons strike a target (outside the nucleus); gamma rays are emitted from the nucleus of a decaying radioactive atom.
distractors: Both are electromagnetic photons, not one particle and one wave.
Gamma rays carry significant energy and penetrate matter.
X-rays readily expose radiographic film.

content.stem: In an X-ray tube, X-rays are produced when:
options: High-speed electrons strike the target (anode)
The cathode filament is cooled right down here
The loaded film is fully developed out here
The whole X-ray tube is fully grounded out here now
content.explanation: Electrons boiled off the filament are accelerated by high voltage and strike the target, where their energy converts to X-rays (and heat).
distractors: Cooling the cathode does not generate X-rays.
Film development is a darkroom process, not X-ray production.
Grounding does not produce X-rays.

content.stem: The continuous X-ray spectrum from a tube is produced by:
options: Bremsstrahlung (electrons decelerating in the target)
Plain nuclear radioactive decay here, somehow oddly
Characteristic radiation only here, somehow quite oddly
Plain visible light emission only here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Bremsstrahlung (braking radiation) gives a continuous spectrum as electrons decelerate near target nuclei; characteristic peaks are superimposed on it.
distractors: Nuclear decay produces gamma rays, not the tube's continuous X-ray spectrum.
Characteristic radiation gives discrete peaks, not the continuous spectrum.
Visible light is not the source of the X-ray spectrum.

content.stem: Characteristic X-rays are produced when:
options: An incident electron ejects an inner-shell electron and an outer electron fills the vacancy
Fast electrons in the tube simply decelerate in the target here, somehow really quite
The source nucleus just decays away here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right
The loaded film just fluoresces brightly here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
content.explanation: Characteristic radiation appears as discrete energy peaks when an inner-shell vacancy is filled by an outer electron, releasing a photon of energy specific to the target element.
distractors: Simple deceleration produces bremsstrahlung, not characteristic peaks.
Nuclear decay produces gamma radiation, not characteristic X-rays.
Film fluorescence is unrelated to characteristic X-ray production.

content.stem: Increasing the kilovoltage (kV) on an X-ray machine primarily increases the radiation's:
options: Energy and penetrating ability
The quantity only here now
The source half-life here now
The film density without limit here
content.explanation: kV controls the energy (quality) of the X-rays, raising their penetrating ability; mA and time control quantity.
distractors: Quantity is controlled mainly by mA and time, not kV.
X-rays from a tube have no half-life; that applies to isotopes.
kV raises penetration and affects density, but density is not unlimited and depends on several factors.

content.stem: Milliamperage (mA) on an X-ray machine primarily controls the:
options: Quantity (intensity) of radiation
The energy of the radiation here
The radioactive source half-life here
The tube focal spot size here
content.explanation: mA sets the tube current and thus the number of X-rays produced (quantity/intensity); kV sets the energy.
distractors: Energy (penetration) is controlled by kV, not mA.
Half-life applies to isotopes, not an X-ray tube.
Focal spot size is a tube design feature, not set by mA.

content.stem: Which is a common industrial gamma-ray source?
options: Iridium-192
Hydrogen-1 here
Carbon-12 now
Lead-208 too
content.explanation: Iridium-192 is a widely used industrial gamma source; Co-60 and Se-75 are also common. The other listed nuclides are stable and non-emitting.
distractors: Hydrogen-1 is stable and not a gamma source.
Carbon-12 is stable and not a gamma source.
Lead-208 is stable; lead is used as shielding, not a source.

content.stem: The approximate half-life of Iridium-192 is:
options: About 74 days
About 5.3 years
About 30 years
About 120 years
content.explanation: Ir-192 has a half-life of roughly 74 days, so its output falls noticeably over weeks and exposure times must be adjusted as it decays.
distractors: About 5.3 years is the half-life of Cobalt-60, not Iridium-192.
About 30 years is the half-life of Cesium-137.
120 years is not the half-life of a common industrial source; Se-75 is about 120 days, not years.

content.stem: The approximate half-life of Cobalt-60 is:
options: About 5.3 years
About 74 days here
About 120 days here
About 30 years too
content.explanation: Co-60 has a half-life of about 5.27 years, giving it a long usable life and high energy suited to thick steel.
distractors: About 74 days is the half-life of Iridium-192.
About 120 days is the half-life of Selenium-75.
About 30 years is the half-life of Cesium-137.

content.stem: The approximate half-life of Selenium-75 is:
options: About 120 days
About 74 days
About 5.3 years
About 30 years
content.explanation: Se-75 has a half-life of about 120 days and a lower average energy, making it useful for thinner steel sections with good sensitivity.
distractors: About 74 days is the half-life of Iridium-192.
About 5.3 years is the half-life of Cobalt-60.
About 30 years is the half-life of Cesium-137.

content.stem: Among common industrial isotopes, which has the highest gamma energy and greatest penetration?
options: Cobalt-60
Selenium-75
Iridium-192
Thulium-170
content.explanation: Co-60 emits about 1.17 and 1.33 MeV gammas (roughly 1.25 MeV average), the highest of these, suited to thick steel; Se-75 is the lowest energy.
distractors: Selenium-75 is among the lowest-energy of these sources.
Iridium-192 is intermediate in energy, below Cobalt-60.
Thulium-170 is a low-energy source for thin sections, not the highest.

content.stem: Cobalt-60 emits gamma rays of approximately:
options: 1.17 and 1.33 MeV
About 0.66 MeV here
About 0.08 to 0.6 MeV
About 0.027 MeV now
content.explanation: Co-60 emits two gammas at about 1.17 and 1.33 MeV (average near 1.25 MeV), giving high penetration for thick steel.
distractors: About 0.66 MeV is the single gamma energy of Cesium-137.
A spread of about 0.08 to 0.6 MeV is closer to the Iridium-192 spectrum.
0.027 MeV is a very low energy, far below Cobalt-60.

content.stem: Iridium-192 emits a spectrum of gamma energies with an average commonly cited around:
options: 0.3 to 0.4 MeV
About 1.25 MeV
About 2.5 MeV now
About 0.01 MeV
content.explanation: Ir-192 emits many gamma lines (roughly 0.2 to 0.6 MeV) with an average often cited near 0.3 to 0.4 MeV, intermediate penetration suited to common steel thicknesses.
distractors: About 1.25 MeV is the average for Cobalt-60, not Iridium-192.
2.5 MeV exceeds the energy of common industrial gamma sources.
0.01 MeV is far too low for Iridium-192.

content.stem: The activity of a radioactive source is measured in:
options: Curies or becquerels
Roentgens only here
Rems only here now
Volts or amperes here
content.explanation: Activity (rate of decay) is expressed in curies (Ci) or becquerels (Bq); 1 Ci equals 3.7 x 10^10 Bq.
distractors: Roentgen is a unit of exposure in air, not activity.
Rem is a unit of dose equivalent, not activity.
Volts measure electrical potential, not activity.

content.stem: One curie is equal to:
options: 3.7 x 10^10 becquerels
About 100 becquerels here
About 1000 becquerels
Just 1 becquerel here
content.explanation: By definition, 1 curie equals 3.7 x 10^10 disintegrations per second, which is 3.7 x 10^10 becquerels.
distractors: 100 Bq is far smaller than a curie.
1000 Bq is far smaller than a curie.
1 Bq is one disintegration per second, vastly smaller than a curie.

content.stem: As a radioactive source decays, its activity:
options: Decreases over time, so exposure times must be increased
Increases steadily over time here, somehow quite oddly
Stays fully constant forever here, somehow quite oddly
Becomes a negative value here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Activity falls as the source decays, so exposure (or source-to-film) settings are adjusted over the source's life to maintain density.
distractors: Activity decreases, not increases, as the source decays.
Activity is not constant; it falls with each half-life.
Activity cannot be negative.

content.stem: Higher specific activity (curies per gram) of a source allows:
options: A physically smaller source, improving radiographic definition
A much larger physical source size here, somehow really quite oddly
A much longer source half-life here, somehow really quite
Much lower beam penetration here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: High specific activity packs more activity into a smaller physical size, reducing the effective focal-spot size and geometric unsharpness for sharper radiographs.
distractors: High specific activity yields a smaller, not larger, source.
Specific activity does not change the isotope's half-life.
Source size does not by itself change the isotope's penetrating energy.

content.stem: The physical size of a gamma source is important because it acts like the:
options: Focal spot, affecting geometric unsharpness
The loaded film's density here, somehow oddly
The beam's half-value layer here, somehow oddly
The developer's temperature here, oddly
content.explanation: The source's physical dimensions behave like an X-ray focal spot; a larger source increases penumbra (geometric unsharpness) and blurs detail.
distractors: Source size is a geometry factor, not film density itself.
Half-value layer is a material/energy property, not source size.
Developer temperature is a processing parameter, unrelated to source size.

content.stem: An advantage of X-ray machines over gamma sources is that:
options: Energy is adjustable and the radiation stops when powered off
They need no electrical power at all here, somehow really quite
They are always far more portable here, somehow really quite
They never ever need any shielding here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: X-ray output can be tuned by kV and switched off entirely, improving control and safety where power is available; gamma sources emit continuously.
distractors: X-ray machines require electrical power.
Gamma projectors are generally more portable than X-ray machines.
X-ray equipment still requires shielding and controls during operation.

content.stem: An advantage of gamma sources over X-ray machines is that they:
options: Are portable and need no electrical power
Can be fully switched off any time here
Always give much higher image definition
Pose no real radiation hazard at all here now
content.explanation: Gamma projectors are compact, need no power, and reach confined field locations, which is why they are common in pipeline and field radiography.
distractors: A gamma source cannot be switched off; it decays continuously.
Gamma sources do not inherently give higher definition; source size and geometry matter.
Gamma sources are a significant radiation hazard requiring strict controls.

content.stem: Because photons have no charge or mass, they:
options: Are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields
Cannot ever penetrate any metal at all here, oddly
Travel far slower than plain sound waves here
Carry a strong positive electric charge here now
content.explanation: Uncharged, massless photons travel in straight lines unaffected by electric or magnetic fields and penetrate matter according to its density and thickness.
distractors: Photons of sufficient energy penetrate metal; that is the basis of RT.
Photons travel at the speed of light, far faster than sound.
Photons carry no charge.

content.stem: Higher photon energy generally results in:
options: Greater penetration through a given material
Much less overall beam penetration here now
A much longer radioactive half-life here
Much lower radioactive source activity here now
content.explanation: More energetic photons penetrate further, so higher energy is used for thicker or denser sections.
distractors: Higher energy increases, not decreases, penetration.
Photon energy does not set an isotope's half-life.
Energy and activity are independent properties.

content.stem: A smaller focal spot on an X-ray tube produces:
options: Sharper images (less geometric unsharpness)
Far more scatter only here, somehow oddly
A higher kV automatically here, somehow oddly
A much longer half-life here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: A smaller focal spot reduces penumbra and geometric unsharpness, improving definition, though it limits how much tube current the target can handle.
distractors: Focal spot size primarily affects sharpness, not scatter level by itself.
Focal spot size does not change the kV.
X-ray tubes have no half-life.

content.stem: Most of the energy delivered to an X-ray tube target becomes:
options: Heat, with only a small fraction becoming X-rays
X-rays, with only very little heat here right now
Plain visible colored light only here right now
Plain audible sound waves only here right now too
content.explanation: X-ray production is inefficient; the great majority of the electron energy becomes heat, which is why targets need cooling and duty cycles are limited.
distractors: Only a small percentage becomes X-rays; most becomes heat.
Little visible light is produced relative to heat.
Sound is not a significant product.

content.stem: Cesium-137 emits a gamma of about 0.66 MeV and has a half-life of about:
options: 30 years
74 days
120 days
5.3 years
content.explanation: Cs-137 has a roughly 30-year half-life and a single 0.662 MeV gamma; it is less common industrially than Ir-192 or Co-60.
distractors: About 74 days is the half-life of Iridium-192.
About 120 days is the half-life of Selenium-75.
About 5.3 years is the half-life of Cobalt-60.

content.stem: For radiography of very thick steel, the preferred gamma source is often:
options: Cobalt-60, for its high energy and penetration
Selenium-75, for its very low energy level here
Thulium-170, for very thin sections here now
Any source at all, since energy does not matter
content.explanation: Co-60's high energy penetrates thick steel where lower-energy sources cannot produce an adequate radiograph.
distractors: Se-75's lower energy suits thinner sections, not very thick steel.
Thulium-170 is for very thin sections.
Energy strongly affects penetration and must match thickness.

content.stem: For thin steel sections where good sensitivity is needed, a lower-energy source such as Selenium-75 is preferred because:
options: Lower energy gives higher subject contrast on thin material
It penetrates thick heavy steel far better here, somehow oddly
It simply has the longest half-life here, somehow quite oddly
It emits no radiation at all here, somehow quite oddly now
content.explanation: Lower-energy photons produce more contrast on thin sections, improving flaw sensitivity where high energy would wash out contrast.
distractors: Lower energy penetrates thick steel less, not better.
Se-75 does not have the longest half-life among common sources.
Se-75 is a radioactive emitter; it is not radiation-free.

content.stem: A gamma source is stored and transported in a shielded device commonly called a:
options: Camera or projector (exposure device)
A film densitometer unit here now
A beam-shaping collimator only here
A loaded film cassette holder here now
content.explanation: The shielded container that houses the source and lets it be cranked out for exposure is the exposure device, also called a camera or projector.
distractors: A densitometer measures film density, not source housing.
A collimator shapes the beam but is not the storage device.
A cassette holds film and screens, not the source.

content.stem: The flexible cable that connects the source to the drive mechanism in a projector is the:
options: Source pigtail / drive cable assembly
A beam-shaping collimator unit here
A film densitometer reading unit here
An IQI penetrameter quality device here
content.explanation: The source capsule is attached to a pigtail/drive cable so it can be cranked from the shielded position out to the exposure position and back.
distractors: A collimator shapes the beam, not the drive connection.
A densitometer measures film density.
An IQI is an image-quality indicator, unrelated to the drive cable.

content.stem: X-rays and gamma rays are called ionizing radiation because they:
options: Can remove electrons from atoms they interact with
They only ever heat up the material here, oddly
They cannot penetrate any matter at all here, oddly
They are fully visible to the naked eye here, oddly
content.explanation: Their energy is high enough to ionize atoms (eject electrons), which underlies both image formation and biological hazard.
distractors: Ionization, not mere heating, defines ionizing radiation.
They do penetrate matter; that is the basis of RT.
X-rays and gamma rays are not visible to the eye.

content.stem: In radiography, radiation 'quality' refers to its:
options: Energy/penetrating ability
Total number of photons here
The film brand only here
The exposure time here
content.explanation: Quality describes the energy (penetrating power) of the beam; quantity describes the number of photons.
distractors: The number of photons is quantity, not quality.
Film brand is unrelated to radiation quality.
Exposure time affects quantity, not the beam's quality.

content.stem: Photon energy in radiography is commonly expressed in:
options: keV or MeV (kilo- or mega-electron-volts)
Curies only here, somehow quite oddly now
Roentgens only here, somehow quite oddly
Becquerels only here, somehow quite oddly now
content.explanation: Photon energy is given in electron-volts, typically keV or MeV; curies and becquerels measure activity and roentgen measures exposure.
distractors: Curie measures source activity, not photon energy.
Roentgen measures exposure in air, not photon energy.
Becquerel measures activity, not photon energy.

content.stem: If an Iridium-192 source has decayed to half its original activity, a previously correct exposure will need:
options: About twice the exposure time (other factors equal)
About half of the exposure time here, somehow oddly
No change at all to it here, somehow really quite oddly
A much higher kV here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: With half the activity, roughly double the time is needed to deliver the same exposure, assuming geometry and other factors are unchanged.
distractors: Halving the time would underexpose the film as activity has dropped.
Decay requires adjustment; no change underexposes the film.
kV applies to X-ray machines, not gamma source decay compensation.

content.stem: The source of electrons in an X-ray tube is the:
options: Heated filament (cathode)
The target anode here now
The beam collimator here
The loaded film sheet here now
content.explanation: The filament at the cathode is heated to release electrons (thermionic emission), which are then accelerated toward the target.
distractors: The target (anode) is where electrons strike to produce X-rays, not their source.
A collimator shapes the beam; it does not emit electrons.
Film records the image; it does not emit electrons.

content.stem: An X-ray tube emits a continuous range of energies up to a maximum set by:
options: The peak kilovoltage applied
The applied tube mA here now
The loaded film type here now
The film developer used here now
content.explanation: The maximum photon energy equals the peak kV; the spectrum is continuous from low energies up to that maximum, with characteristic peaks added.
distractors: mA controls quantity, not the maximum energy.
Film type does not set the X-ray energy.
The developer is a processing chemical, unrelated to the spectrum.

content.stem: Unlike an X-ray machine, a gamma source emits radiation:
options: Continuously and at fixed energies that cannot be adjusted
Only ever when it is fully powered here, somehow oddly
At a fully adjustable energy level here, somehow oddly
Never at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed now
content.explanation: A gamma source decays continuously at energies fixed by the isotope; you cannot turn it off or tune its energy, only shield it.
distractors: Gamma sources do not require power and cannot be powered off.
Gamma energies are fixed by the isotope, not adjustable.
Gamma sources do emit; they cannot be switched off.

content.stem: The SI unit of radioactivity is the:
options: Becquerel
The Curie
The Gray now
Sievert
content.explanation: The becquerel (Bq), one decay per second, is the SI unit of activity; the curie is the older unit.
distractors: The curie is the traditional (non-SI) unit of activity.
The gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose, not activity.
The sievert is the SI unit of dose equivalent, not activity.

content.stem: Different isotopes are kept available because:
options: Energy must be matched to material type and thickness
All of the sources are fully identical here, somehow oddly
Only one single thickness is ever radiographed here
The radioactive half-life does not matter at all here
content.explanation: Source energy is selected to suit the material and thickness for adequate penetration and contrast, so a range of isotopes covers different jobs.
distractors: Sources differ in energy and half-life; they are not identical.
Many thicknesses are radiographed, requiring different energies.
Half-life affects source life and exposure planning, so it matters.

content.stem: Which pairing of source and relative energy is correct?
options: Co-60 high, Ir-192 medium, Se-75 lower
Se-75 highest, then Co-60 lowest here
All three have fully identical energy
Ir-192 highest of the whole three here
content.explanation: Among these, Co-60 has the highest energy, Ir-192 is intermediate, and Se-75 is lower, which guides thickness selection.
distractors: Se-75 is the lowest, not highest, and Co-60 is the highest.
These sources have distinctly different energies.
Co-60, not Ir-192, has the highest energy of the three.

content.stem: The half-life of an isotope is the time for its:
options: Activity to decay to half its value
Its energy to fully double here
Its source size to fully halve here now
Its film density to halve here now
content.explanation: Half-life is the period over which activity falls to one half; it is fixed for each isotope and governs source replacement and exposure planning.
distractors: Half-life concerns activity decay, not energy doubling.
Physical source size does not halve with half-life.
Film density is an imaging result, not what half-life measures.

content.stem: After two half-lives, a source's activity is about:
options: One quarter of the original
One half of the original
One eighth of the original
Left fully unchanged here now
content.explanation: Each half-life halves the activity, so after two half-lives the activity is one half of one half, which is one quarter.
distractors: One half is the activity after a single half-life, not two.
One eighth corresponds to three half-lives, not two.
Activity decreases with each half-life; it does not stay unchanged.

content.stem: Compared with a low-kV X-ray exposure of thin steel, an Iridium-192 exposure of the same part typically gives:
options: Lower contrast because of its higher average energy
Much higher subject contrast here, somehow oddly
Fully identical final results here, somehow oddly
No real image at all here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Ir-192's higher average energy yields lower subject contrast on thin steel than an optimized low-kV X-ray exposure, which is why X-ray is often preferred for thin, critical work.
distractors: The higher-energy gamma source gives lower, not higher, contrast on thin steel.
The two are not identical; energy spectra differ.

content.stem: When a radioactive source decays, it:
options: Transforms toward a more stable nuclide while emitting radiation
It simply gains more activity here, somehow really quite oddly enough
It just becomes an X-ray tube here, somehow really quite oddly
It stops being radioactive instantly here, somehow quite oddly
content.explanation: Radioactive decay converts the unstable nucleus toward a more stable state, emitting gamma (and other) radiation in the process.
distractors: Decay reduces activity over time; it does not gain activity.
A source does not become an X-ray tube.

content.stem: A key safety distinction of gamma sources is that they:
options: Cannot be turned off and must be shielded at all times
They emit only ever when energized here, somehow oddly
They are fully harmless when stored here, somehow oddly
They produce no penetrating radiation here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Because a gamma source emits continuously, it must remain shielded in its device and controlled at all times; it cannot be switched off like an X-ray machine.
distractors: Gamma sources are not energized; they emit by decay regardless of power.

content.stem: As radiation passes through a material, its intensity is:
options: Attenuated (reduced) by absorption and scatter
Greatly increased here, somehow really quite oddly
Left fully unchanged here, somehow really quite oddly
Fully converted into sound here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: The beam is attenuated as photons are absorbed or scattered out of it; thicker or denser material attenuates more, which is what forms the radiographic image.
distractors: Intensity decreases through material; it does not increase.
Intensity changes with thickness and density; it is not unchanged.
Radiation energy is not converted to sound.

content.stem: A half-value layer (HVL) is the thickness of material that:
options: Reduces the radiation intensity to one half
Fully doubles the whole intensity here now
Stops all of the radiation fully here now
Has no real effect on the intensity here now
content.explanation: One HVL cuts the beam intensity in half; HVL depends on the material and the radiation energy and is a key shielding and exposure concept.
distractors: An HVL halves, it does not double, intensity.
One HVL halves intensity; it does not stop all radiation.
An HVL by definition reduces intensity.

content.stem: For a given material, higher-energy radiation has an HVL that is:
options: Thicker (more material needed to halve it)
Much thinner here, somehow really quite oddly
Fully zero here, somehow really quite
A negative value here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Higher-energy photons penetrate more, so more material is needed to halve them; the HVL increases with energy.
distractors: Higher energy needs more, not less, material to halve it.
HVL is never zero for real materials.
Thickness cannot be negative.

content.stem: Two half-value layers reduce the beam intensity to about:
options: One quarter
One half here
One eighth
Zero now
content.explanation: Each HVL halves the beam, so two HVLs give one half of one half, which is one quarter.
distractors: One half results from a single HVL, not two.
One eighth corresponds to three HVLs.
Two HVLs do not reduce intensity to zero.

content.stem: A tenth-value layer (TVL) reduces beam intensity to:
options: One tenth
One half
One hundredth
One quarter
content.explanation: A TVL cuts intensity to one tenth; it is convenient for shielding calculations since each TVL removes 90 percent of the remaining beam.
distractors: Halving corresponds to an HVL, not a TVL.
One hundredth corresponds to two TVLs.
One quarter corresponds to two HVLs.

content.stem: The photoelectric effect is most significant at:
options: Lower photon energies and in higher-atomic-number materials
Only at very high energies here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Only ever at zero energy here, somehow really quite oddly now
Only above the pair production threshold here, somehow
content.explanation: Photoelectric absorption dominates at lower energies and rises sharply with atomic number, which is why it contributes strongly to contrast on dense materials at low kV.
distractors: Photoelectric absorption falls off, not rises, at very high energies.
There is no interaction at zero energy.
Pair production is the high-energy process, not photoelectric.

content.stem: Compton scattering is the dominant interaction at:
options: Intermediate energies typical of much industrial radiography
Only ever at the very lowest energies here, somehow oddly
Only ever above 1.02 MeV here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Only ever at zero energy here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Compton scattering dominates across the intermediate energy range common in industrial RT; it produces scattered radiation that degrades image quality.
distractors: The lowest energies favor the photoelectric effect.
Above about 1.02 MeV pair production begins to contribute, but Compton dominates the mid range.
There is no interaction at zero energy.

content.stem: Pair production can occur only when the photon energy exceeds about:
options: 1.02 MeV
0.5 MeV here
0.1 MeV now
10 keV too
content.explanation: Pair production requires at least 1.02 MeV (twice the electron rest-mass energy) to create an electron-positron pair, so it matters mainly for high-energy sources like Co-60 and high-MeV machines.
distractors: 0.5 MeV is below the 1.02 MeV threshold for pair production.

content.stem: Scattered radiation reaching the film generally:
options: Reduces contrast and degrades image quality
Greatly improves the whole contrast here
Has no real effect on it at all here now
Greatly increases the whole definition here
content.explanation: Scatter adds a general fog that lowers contrast and sensitivity, so radiographers work to reduce and control it.
distractors: Scatter lowers, not improves, contrast.
Scatter does affect the radiograph by adding fog.

content.stem: Backscatter from objects behind the film is commonly controlled by:
options: A lead sheet behind the cassette
Greatly increasing the kV here
Removing all of the filters here
A much longer development time here
content.explanation: A lead sheet behind the film absorbs backscatter; a lead 'B' that appears as a light image on the film warns that backscatter is excessive.
distractors: Raising kV can increase scatter, not control backscatter.
Removing filters does not address backscatter.
Development time does not control backscatter.

content.stem: If a lead letter 'B' placed behind the cassette appears as a lighter image on the radiograph, it indicates:
options: Excessive backscatter, and the radiograph may be unacceptable
Fully correct beam exposure here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Good overall image contrast here, somehow really quite oddly enough

The whole total exposure time used here

Just the same as the film side here, somehow really quite oddly enough now

content.stem: Choosing between single-wall and double-wall techniques depends mainly on:

Only the developer temperature here, somehow really quite
Only the operator's preference alone here, somehow really quite

Selection is governed by geometry and code, not preference alone.

The whole densitometer alone here, somehow oddly
The whole survey meter here, somehow really quite
The whole source serial number here, oddly

Indicate the whole image quality here, somehow oddly
Show the required sensitivity here, somehow quite oddly now

Showing the required sensitivity is the IQI's purpose.
Confirming contrast and definition is part of its role.

content.stem: On a long radiograph with varying thickness, codes may require:
options: More than one IQI to represent the range of thicknesses
No IQI at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
Only a film-side IQI here, somehow really quite oddly enough
An IQI on the densitometer here, somehow really quite

Source-side placement is preferred where accessible, not film side by default.
The IQI goes on the part, not the densitometer.

content.stem: Hole-type and wire-type IQIs:
options: Are alternative IQI designs, selected per the governing code
Cannot both ever indicate the sensitivity here, somehow
Are exactly the same device here, somehow really quite oddly enough

They are different designs, not identical.
Neither is a dosimeter.

content.stem: The elliptical (DWDI) technique on small pipe typically requires:
options: Two exposures about 90 degrees apart to cover the full weld
Just one single exposure only here, somehow really quite oddly
No location markers at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough
A whole panoramic source here, somehow really quite oddly

options: Acceptable geometric unsharpness and weld coverage per the technique
Much higher overall film fog here, somehow really quite oddly enough now
A far shorter exposure always here, somehow really quite oddly enough now
No need for an IQI at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough

content.stem: Location markers should be placed on the part such that:
options: Their position on the film unambiguously locates indications on the part
They never ever appear on the film at all here, somehow really quite oddly
They fully cover the whole weld here, somehow really quite oddly enough now
They fully replace the whole IQI here, somehow really quite oddly enough

Markers must not obscure the weld.
Markers do not replace the IQI.

content.stem: If the required IQI level is not visible, the radiographer should:
options: Adjust technique (energy, exposure, geometry, scatter control) and reshoot
Just fully accept the film here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
Just erase the whole IQI here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
Just increase the ambient light here, somehow really quite oddly enough

Ambient light is a viewing condition, not a fix for technique sensitivity.

content.stem: Without a shim under the IQI on a weld with reinforcement, the IQI may:
options: Represent less than the actual examined thickness, overstating sensitivity
Just represent far more whole thickness here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Have no real effect at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
Just become a plain dosimeter here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: If the IQI sits on base metal thinner than the weld plus reinforcement, it represents less thickness and can overstate the achieved sensitivity, so a shim is used.
distractors: Without a shim it represents less, not more, thickness.
It does affect how sensitivity is represented.
An IQI is not a dosimeter.

content.stem: The radiographic technique (energy, SFD, IQI, geometry) should be:
options: Documented so the examination is repeatable and traceable
Kept only ever in the operator's memory here, somehow oddly
Changed on each single film fully at random here, oddly
Hidden away from the whole review here, somehow really quite

distractors: Relying on memory is not acceptable documentation.
Random changes undermine repeatability.
Technique records support, not avoid, review.

content.stem: For a hole-type IQI, the plaque thickness is normally a small percentage of the:
options: Specimen (part) thickness being radiographed
The whole source size here, somehow quite oddly
The whole film thickness here, somehow oddly
The developer volume here, somehow quite oddly
content.explanation: The plaque is a defined percentage (commonly about 2 percent) of the part thickness, so the IQI scales with the section examined.
distractors: It scales with part thickness, not source size.
It is not based on film thickness.
It is unrelated to developer volume.

content.stem: For a hole-type IQI to be valid, the interpreter must be able to see:
options: The IQI outline and the essential hole
Only the whole lead numbers here now
Only the whole part edge here right now
The whole survey meter unit here now
content.explanation: The IQI body and the required (essential) hole must be visible on the radiograph to confirm the sensitivity level was met.
distractors: The identification numbers alone do not demonstrate the hole sensitivity.
The part edge is not the sensitivity indicator.
A survey meter is unrelated to film interpretation.

content.stem: In the elliptical technique, offsetting the beam is done to:
options: Separate the near and far weld images so both can be interpreted
Greatly increase the whole scatter here, somehow really quite oddly
Greatly shorten the exposure here, somehow really quite oddly
Fully remove the whole IQI here, somehow really quite oddly enough

distractors: The offset is for image separation, not to increase scatter.
It does not shorten exposure.
An IQI is still required.

content.stem: Which technique suits a large-diameter pipe with internal source access?
options: Panoramic single-wall exposure
Elliptical DWDI
Double-wall single-image from outside only
No radiography is possible
content.explanation: With internal access on a large pipe, a panoramic single-wall exposure images the full weld efficiently in one shot.
distractors: The elliptical technique is for small-diameter pipe.
DWSI from outside is used when internal access is unavailable.
Radiography is possible with appropriate technique.

content.stem: Wire IQIs are oriented so the wires:
options: Lie across the weld/area of interest as required by the code
Run right along the whole source cable here, somehow really quite
Are fully hidden behind the lead here, somehow really quite oddly
Point right at the survey meter here, somehow really quite

distractors: Orientation follows the code relative to the weld, not the source cable.
The IQI must be visible, not hidden behind lead.
Orientation has nothing to do with a survey meter.

content.stem: Which statement about IQIs is correct?
options: They demonstrate technique sensitivity and are normally placed source-side in the area of interest
They directly measure the whole actual flaw depth all on their own here, somehow really quite oddly
They are always placed only ever on the film side of the part here, somehow really quite oddly enough
They are simply plain radiation dosimeters in every case here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: IQIs show the technique met the required sensitivity and are normally placed on the source side within the area of interest; film-side placement is the marked exception.
distractors: IQIs do not directly measure flaw depth.
Source-side is the default; film-side is the exception.
IQIs are not dosimeters.

content.stem: On a radiograph, a discontinuity that removes material (such as a void) appears:
options: Darker than the surrounding sound metal
Lighter than the surrounding sound metal
The exact same density as the metal here
Fully invisible at any density here now
content.explanation: Less material in the path lets more radiation through, darkening that area of the film; voids, porosity, and most volumetric flaws image as darker spots.
distractors: Lighter areas correspond to more material or denser inclusions, not voids.
A void changes local density, so it differs from sound metal.
Adequate technique makes such discontinuities visible.

content.stem: A high-density inclusion such as tungsten in a weld appears on film as:
options: A lighter (lower-density) spot
A much darker spot here now
No indication at all here now
Just a fine hairline crack here now
content.explanation: A tungsten inclusion absorbs more radiation than the surrounding metal, so less reaches the film and the spot images lighter.
distractors: Darker areas indicate less material; a dense inclusion does the opposite.
A dense inclusion does produce an indication.
It is a rounded dense indication, not a crack.

options: Rounded dark spots, individually or in clusters
Straight light lines here, somehow quite oddly
A uniform light band here, somehow quite oddly
No indication at all here, somehow really quite oddly

Porosity produces visible dark indications.

Bright rounded dots here, somehow really quite oddly
A light line at the whole root here, somehow really quite oddly
Nothing at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed

distractors: Slag is dark and irregular, not bright rounded dots (which suggest dense inclusions).
A light root line suggests a dense feature, not slag.
Slag produces visible dark indications.

content.stem: Lack of fusion (LOF) often appears on a radiograph as:

Just a single bright spot here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
Just a rounded void only here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
Just a uniform density here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here now

LOF produces a local density change, not uniform density.

content.stem: Incomplete (lack of) penetration in a groove weld typically appears as:
options: A straight dark line at the weld root
A bright rounded weld spot here now
Scattered light dots all over here now
No real indication at all here right now

It produces a visible indication.

Perpendicular to the whole beam here, somehow oddly
Always, regardless of the orientation here now
Only ever when fully filled with slag here now

Rounded dense spots here, somehow really quite
A uniform light area here, somehow really quite oddly

A fine straight line only here, somehow really quite
No indication at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough

Just a dark void here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Just a fine crack here, somehow really quite oddly
Just porosity here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed

Just a bright centerline here, somehow really
Rounded dense inclusions here, somehow really quite oddly
No density change here, somehow really quite oddly enough

Just plain metal riveting here now

A single crack
Lack of penetration

Plain excess reinforcement here
Plain root concavity only here now

Straight light lines here, somehow really
No indication at all here, somehow really quite oddly

A single straight light line here, somehow
Just uniform density here, somehow really quite oddly

Just excess thickness here, somehow really quite oddly

Just rounded dense spots here, somehow really quite oddly enough

No indication at all here, somehow really quite oddly

Just a dense bright area here, somehow really quite
Just a crack at the root here, somehow really
Just porosity only here, somehow really quite oddly

The whole density does not matter here, somehow really quite

Never ever detectable here, somehow really quite oddly

content.stem: The main visual cue separating slag from porosity on film is that slag is usually:

Just always fully rounded here, somehow really quite oddly
Always lighter than the whole metal here, somehow really quite

Lack of penetration (a whole gap) here

Burn-through (lost metal) here now

Just darker than the whole slag here, somehow really
Identically to the whole slag here, somehow really quite oddly
Just as a crack here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed

content.stem: Discontinuity length on a radiograph is commonly measured using:

Only ever the whole densitometer reading here, somehow really quite
Only ever the whole kV setting here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Only the source activity here, somehow really quite oddly

content.stem: Codes often distinguish scattered porosity from clustered porosity because:

The whole outer color simply differs here, somehow really quite oddly
It changes the whole source energy here, somehow really quite oddly
It is fully non-relevant here, somehow really quite oddly enough

Just the whole weld cap only here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right now
Just the outer surface only here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right now
The exact same location here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right now

content.stem: Radiography is well suited to volumetric flaws but, compared with ultrasonic testing, is generally less reliable for:
options: Detecting tight, planar flaws oriented across the beam
Just detecting plain porosity here, somehow really
Just detecting plain slag here, somehow really quite oddly
Just detecting density changes here, somehow really quite

RT detects slag well.

content.stem: The roentgen (R) is a unit of:
options: Radiation exposure in air
Plain absorbed dose here
Plain dose equivalent here
Plain source activity here now

The roentgen
The curie

options: Rem or sievert
The rad or gray here
The roentgen here
The curie here

distractors: Rad and gray measure absorbed dose, not dose equivalent.

The curie measures activity.

1 rad
10 rad

distractors: 1 sievert is 100 rem, not 1 rem.
1 sievert is 100 rem, not 10 rem.
1 sievert is 100 rem, not 1000 rem.

content.stem: The three cardinal rules of radiation protection are:
options: Time, distance, and shielding
Develop, fix, then wash here
kV, mA, and the time here
Source, film, and the IQI here

distractors: Develop, fix, wash are film processing steps, not protection rules.
kV, mA, time are exposure factors, not protection rules.

content.stem: Reducing the time spent near a radiation source:
options: Proportionally reduces the dose received
Greatly increases the whole dose here
Has no real effect on the dose at all here
Greatly changes the source energy here

distractors: Less time reduces, not increases, dose.
Time directly affects accumulated dose.
Time does not change the source's energy.

content.stem: Increasing distance from a source reduces dose rate according to the:
options: Inverse square law
Half-life
Reciprocity law
Characteristic curve
content.explanation: Dose rate falls with the square of distance, so distance is one of the most effective protective measures.
distractors: Half-life concerns source decay over time, not distance.
Reciprocity relates intensity and time for film exposure.
The characteristic curve relates film density to log exposure.

content.stem: ALARA stands for:
options: As Low As Reasonably Achievable
Always Limit All Radiation Access
Approved Levels And Radiation Allowances
Automatic Logging And Recording Activity
content.explanation: ALARA is the principle of keeping radiation doses as low as reasonably achievable, below regulatory limits, considering technology and cost.
distractors: This is not the meaning of ALARA.
This is not the meaning of ALARA.
This is not the meaning of ALARA.

content.stem: Under US NRC regulations (10 CFR 20), the annual occupational whole-body dose limit is:

50 rem (0.5 Sv)

options: 0.1 rem (100 mrem)
Just 5 rem here now
Just 50 rem here now
Just 1 rem only here now

content.stem: A 'radiation area' is generally defined as an area where a person could receive a dose rate exceeding:
options: 5 mrem in one hour at 30 cm
100 rem in one whole hour here
5 rem in one hour at 30 cm here
0.1 mrem in one whole hour here

5 rem in one hour at 30 cm is far above the radiation-area threshold.
0.1 mrem in one hour is below the radiation-area threshold.

options: 100 mrem in one hour at 30 cm
5 mrem in one whole hour here
1 mrem in one whole hour here
5 rem in one whole hour here now
content.explanation: Per 10 CFR 20, a high radiation area is one where the dose could exceed about 100 mrem (0.1 rem) in one hour at 30 cm. (Verify against the current regulation.)

1 mrem in one hour is below the radiation-area threshold.
5 rem in one hour is well above the high-radiation-area threshold.

content.stem: A survey meter (such as a Geiger-Mueller or ion chamber instrument) is used to:
options: Measure radiation dose rate in an area
Record the cumulative personal dose here
Develop out the whole loaded film here
Set the whole tube kV level here right now
content.explanation: Survey meters read the dose rate at a location, used to establish boundaries and confirm the source is shielded; personal cumulative dose is tracked by dosimeters.
distractors: Cumulative personal dose is recorded by dosimeters, not survey meters.
Survey meters do not develop film.

options: Measuring higher dose rates accurately
Detecting single low counts here now
Recording the whole personal dose here
Developing out the whole loaded film here
content.explanation: Ion chambers handle higher dose-rate fields well, while GM instruments are very sensitive at low levels; the right instrument is chosen for the field.
distractors: Detecting individual low-level counts is a GM strength, not the ion chamber's advantage.

content.stem: A film badge or TLD/OSL dosimeter is worn to:

Read the whole instantaneous dose rate here, oddly

Measure the whole source activity here, oddly
Develop out the whole loaded film here, oddly
Set the whole exposure time here, somehow oddly

It does not set exposure parameters.

Measure the whole film density here, somehow really quite oddly

Just develop out the film first here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Greatly increase the source activity here, somehow really quite oddly

Approach the source immediately to pull it out by hand here, somehow oddly
Just ignore it all and continue here, somehow really quite oddly enough

Just far faster film processing here, somehow
Just a much higher tube kV here, somehow really quite
Just a lower cost only here, somehow really quite oddly

Only warms the whole tissue harmlessly here
Cannot interact with the whole tissue here

Just the whole survey meter here, somehow really quite oddly

Its brightness compared to the surrounding film as well
Its position relative to the start of the weld

Too large a root opening set in the bevel alone
Misalignment of the abutting pipe ends at the root

The color tone it shows on the processed film
The angle it makes relative to the weld axis

Missing right across the entire weld cross section

It appears only along the finished weld cap region
Its density does not exceed that of the thinnest adjacent base metal

content.stem: A burn-through on an API 1104 radiograph is evaluated by its:
options: Its brightness compared to the film border edge on the joint
Its size relative to the wall thickness, density considered
Its distance from the nearest scattered pore
The number of repair passes laid down nearby

content.stem: Elongated slag inclusions are judged primarily by their:

Their distance measured from the start of the weld itself
Their length and the aggregate length over a weld length
The overall film density read across the weld

Density alone does not size slag.

Their spacing measured back from the weld cap
The exposure time that was used on the shot
Their width in addition to their length

content.stem: Scattered (individual) porosity on an API 1104 radiograph is assessed by:

The color of each individual pore on the film on the joint
Their distance from the stenciled pipe number
The film border density around the radiograph

Confined strictly to the weld root region only
Grouped in a localized cluster, judged as a group
Acceptable without any size or length limit

content.explanation: Cluster porosity is a localized group of pores evaluated against its own size/length limit rather than as scattered porosity.

content.stem: Hollow-bead (elongated root) porosity is controlled mainly by its:
options: Its color as it registers on the processed film
Its individual length and aggregate length in the root
Its distance measured down from the weld cap
The total film area the radiograph happens to cover itself
distractors: Color is not measured.
Cap distance is not the parameter.
Film area is unrelated to acceptance.
content.explanation: Hollow bead is a root condition limited by individual length and total length over the reference weld length.

content.stem: The 'accumulation of imperfections' provision in API 1104 limits the:
options: The number of radiographs taken across each joint as well
The count of repair welders working on the site
Total length of imperfections within a given weld length
The film density measured at the very weld edge
distractors: It governs imperfections, not radiograph count.
It is not a personnel provision.
It is not a density rule.
content.explanation: The accumulation rule caps the combined length of several imperfections falling within a specified continuous weld length.

content.stem: Undercut adjacent to the weld is often dispositioned in API 1104 by:
options: The film color alone as developed on the shot
The stenciled pipe heat number near the joint
The number of weld passes used to fill the joint itself
Its depth, assessed by visual or mechanical means
distractors: Color is not the acceptance parameter.
Heat number does not size undercut.
Pass count does not set undercut limits.
content.explanation: Undercut is depth-controlled and is commonly evaluated by visual or mechanical measurement in addition to the radiograph, with separate limits.

content.stem: Aggregate length limits for several imperfection types are summed over a:
options: A single radiographic film frame on its own
A specified continuous length of the weld
The full joint length regardless of its size
A fixed number of pores counted on the film
distractors: The basis is a weld length, not one film frame.
It is a defined length, not the whole joint.
Pore count is not the aggregation basis.
content.explanation: Several discontinuity limits are expressed as a total length permitted within a specified continuous length of weld.

content.stem: For several discontinuity types, the API 1104 length limits are tied to the:
options: The ambient temperature recorded during the shot
The film manufacturer that supplied the stock
The nominal weld or wall thickness of the joint
The size of the crew running the radiography
distractors: Temperature is a process condition, not an acceptance variable.
Film brand does not set acceptance.
Crew size is unrelated.
content.explanation: Limits for some discontinuities scale with the nominal wall thickness of the joint.

content.stem: Acceptance limits for an indication found by ultrasonic testing under API 1104 are:
options: Identical to the radiographic limits in every case
Defined separately from the radiographic limits
Drawn directly from ASME Section V provisions
Set per job by the technician on the spread
distractors: RT and UT acceptance are not interchangeable.
Section V is a method document, not the acceptance source here.
Acceptance follows the standard, not ad hoc settings.
content.explanation: API 1104 gives method-specific acceptance; UT carries its own provisions distinct from the radiographic workmanship limits.

content.stem: Before a radiograph can be evaluated to API 1104 criteria, it must first meet requirements for:
options: The seniority of the welder who made the joint
Image quality, including penetrameter (IQI) sensitivity
The color of the coating applied to the pipe
The length of the crew's working shift that day as a rule
distractors: Personnel seniority is not a film-quality factor.
Coating color does not affect film validity.
Shift length is irrelevant to image quality.
content.explanation: A radiograph must demonstrate adequate sensitivity, shown by the required IQI/penetrameter, before indications are dispositioned.

content.stem: A valid API 1104 radiograph must fall within a specified range of:
options: Film density measured through the area of interest
Ambient humidity recorded at the shooting position
The source-to-film cost charged for the shot
The operator's stenciled certification number
distractors: Humidity is not a film-acceptance parameter.
Cost is unrelated to validity.
A certification number does not validate density.
content.explanation: The radiograph's density through the weld must sit inside an allowed range for the image to be evaluable.

content.stem: After a rejected section is repaired, the weld is:
options: Accepted on the strength of the repair note alone
Re-examined by the same method and acceptance criteria
Judged the second time by noticeably relaxed criteria itself
Cut out and the joint rewelded in every single case
distractors: A repair still requires NDT.
Criteria do not relax for repairs.
Cut-out is not automatic for every repair.
content.explanation: A repair is re-inspected to the same NDT method and acceptance standard as the original examination.

content.stem: Whether a given defect may be repaired at all under API 1104 depends on:
options: The defect type and the company's repair provisions
The particular time of day the weld was made
The personal preference of the radiographer present
The brand of film stock loaded in the cassette
distractors: Timing does not govern repairability.
It is set by the standard and company, not preference.
Film brand is irrelevant.
content.explanation: Some defects may be repaired and others require removal; cracks in particular have restricted repair provisions, and repeat repairs may be limited.

content.stem: In API 1104 usage, an indication that exceeds the acceptance criteria is termed a:
options: Discontinuity present anywhere in the weld
Geometric unsharpness across the radiograph
Defect
Penetrameter placed beside the weld
distractors: A discontinuity is any interruption, acceptable or not.
Unsharpness is an image-quality term.
A penetrameter is an image-quality indicator.
content.explanation: A discontinuity becomes a defect only when it exceeds the applicable acceptance criteria and is rejectable.

content.stem: Final acceptance or rejection of a weld against API 1104 rests with the:
options: The company, applying the standard's criteria
The radiographer who processed the film alone
The pipe mill that originally supplied the joint
The film processor that ran the development
distractors: The radiographer reports; disposition is the company's.
The mill supplies pipe, not weld disposition.
Processing the film does not decide acceptance.
content.explanation: The company is responsible for accepting, repairing, or rejecting a weld based on the standard's criteria, informed by the NDT results.

content.stem: NDT used to show compliance with API 1104 must be performed by personnel who are:
options: Members of the welding crew on the spread
Qualified and certified for the radiographic method
Approved by the coating crew on the line
Selected by lottery from the available hands as well
distractors: Performing welders are not the NDT authority.
Coating approval is unrelated to NDT qualification.
Qualification is by certification, not chance.
content.explanation: Examinations are carried out by qualified, certified NDT personnel under the applicable qualification provisions.
